title: State of Data — Sean Cai, Independent / State of Data

primary.label: AI Data Engineering
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 94%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk is a cross-domain analysis of the AI data market itself — it references finance, coding, healthcare, law, cybersecurity, biology, and robotics as illustrative verticals but the primary subject is the data and eval landscape that applies across all of them. No single application vertical is the focus.

domains.label: Finance & Trading
domains.rationale: Finance serves as the concrete demonstration domain: three real finance tasks (ARR waterfall reconciliation, LBO valuation memo, long-short pair trade) are benchmarked with deterministic verifiers to expose benchmark psychosis and divergent failure modes between GPT 5.5 and Opus 4.8. Finance is the most substantial specific vertical discussed.

domains.label: Data & Analytics
domains.rationale: The talk is fundamentally about data markets, data pipelines, data quality, and the economics of data as an asset class. While 'data and analytics' in the taxonomy refers to analytics/BI/data-agent products rather than the data supply chain itself, the thematic overlap is substantial.

summary: Sean Cai reframes AI data markets beyond traditional annotation rooms toward the scarce asset: process data that converts generalist models into domain experts. He distinguishes type one data (real captured workflows with minimal shaping) from type two data (contrived expert-manufactured examples), noting that type one drives 20-to-80% performance gains while vendors routinely mislabel type two as type one. Invoking Jason Wei's Verifier's Law—the ease of training a model is proportional to how verifiable the task is—Cai decomposes verifiability into three axes (asymmetry, veracity, proliferation) and predicts markets mature in verifiability order: code → search → finance → healthcare/law → cyber/bio/science → taste. He attacks contrived benchmarks as Goodhart's-law failures, demonstrating with three finance tasks (ARR waterfall reconciliation, LBO valuation memo, long-short pair trade) where GPT 5.5 and Opus 4.8 scored within three points while failing oppositely—GPT nailed arithmetic, Opus nailed methodology—revealing post-training direction divergences hidden by single benchmark numbers. Data market spending serves as an upstream indicator of lab product launches: Anthropic's cybersecurity spending in January and biological data spending in March/April preceded Metis, Cybor, and Claude bio/life sciences launches by 2-3 months. Robotics serves as a counterexample where modality remains unsettled (ego vs teleop vs UMI) and vendors are unsophisticated. Cai argues no infrastructure pioneer has held more than 10% market long-term, and GLM 5.2 surpassing GPT on real-world rubrics proves app-layer companies can decouple from model labs. Successful data companies are pivoting to enterprise as 'neo labs,' building abstraction layers for model routing by latency and performance, RL dataset management across base model migration with automatic post-training reruns, and Antikythera mechanisms that translate messy business context into runnable eval suites with deterministic verifiers. The durable moat is a live pipeline into real work plus retraining infrastructure, not static datasets. Cai announces a new venture offering RL as a service for enterprises, working with real-world companies to monetize data assets.
whyItMatters: The talk weaves data engineering, evaluation methodology, and market analysis into a unified framework. Process data classification (type one vs type two) connects directly to verifiability (Verifier's Law) because verifiability determines which data can be effectively captured, verified, and used for post-training. Benchmark pathology (Goodhart's law, benchmark psychosis, hill-climbing) demonstrates why current evaluation fails to measure real expertise, which in turn explains why live data pipelines and retraining infrastructure—not static datasets or single benchmark scores—constitute durable moats. The market maturation ordering (code → search → finance → healthcare/law → cyber/bio/science → taste) emerges from the intersection of verifiability axes and data availability, while the infrastructure pioneer thesis (>10% ceiling) explains why app-layer companies can decouple from model labs via model routing and RL-as-a-service architectures. Together, these concepts argue that the scarce resource in AI is not compute or models but verifiable process data from real workflows, and that durable value accrues to those who build the Antikythera mechanisms, live pipelines, and retraining infrastructure to capture and continuously learn from it. The robotics counterexample and finance benchmark demonstration ground the framework in concrete cases where the theory either predicts accurately (finance benchmark divergence) or fails (robotics modality uncertainty), making the overall framework falsifiable rather than purely theoretical.
temporalContext: Published July 26, 2026. The talk references model versions GPT 5.5, Opus 4.7, Opus 4.8, and GLM 5.2, and discusses events from late 2025 through mid-2026: Anthropic's cybersecurity data spending in January 2026 and biological data spending in March/April 2026 preceding Claude bio/life sciences product launches by 2-3 months. Jason Wei's Verifier's Law blog post was published July 15, 2025, and the academic paper citing it (arXiv:2509.17995) appeared September 2025. Scale AI's $1B Series F was May 2024 and Meta's 49% minority investment was June 2025. The talk was delivered during a period of rapid model iteration, data market unbundling, and enterprise AI deployment scaling in mid-2026, with CapEx spending exponentially increasing while AI revenues lagged.

concepts.name: Verifier's Law (verification asymmetry)
concepts.explanation: Jason Wei's principle that the ease of training a model to do a task is proportional to how verifiable the task is. All tasks that are possible to solve and easy to verify will be solved by AI. Originated in Wei's July 2025 blog post and independently cited in academic literature.
concepts.importance: Central conceptual framework of the talk. It provides the predictive model for which AI application markets will mature first and underpins the entire data market analysis.

concepts.name: Three axes of verifiability
concepts.explanation: Cai decomposes verifiability into three dimensions: asymmetry (verification easier than generation), veracity (ground truth reliability), and proliferation (scalability of verification). Coding scored high on all three via GitHub, explaining why code matured first.
concepts.importance: Operationalizes Verifier's Law into a practical framework for ranking AI application domains by their likelihood of rapid maturation, guiding investment and engineering prioritization.

concepts.name: Goodhart's law in AI benchmarks
concepts.explanation: When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. Cai applies this to AI benchmarks: vendors hire experts to generate tasks, cherry-pick divergences, package them as hard benchmarks, then sell data to hill-climb those same benchmarks—Goodhart's law with profit.
concepts.importance: Explains the systemic failure of the AI evaluation ecosystem where benchmark creators have financial incentives to make benchmarks gameable, undermining evaluation validity.

concepts.name: Benchmark psychosis
concepts.explanation: Cai's term for the pathology of treating a single benchmark number under a single scaffold as meaningful, when it is actually one noisy sample from an unmeasured distribution. Hidden false positive and false negative rates further undermine benchmark head stats.
concepts.importance: A cautionary concept for AI engineers: relying on single benchmark numbers leads to systematically misleading conclusions about model capability and failure modes.

concepts.name: Hill-climbing benchmarks
concepts.explanation: The practice of creating a benchmark, then selling the data to hill-climb that same benchmark. Vendors generate contrived tasks, package them as benchmarks, and then monetize the data needed to game them, creating a circular incentive structure.
concepts.importance: Identifies a specific mechanism of benchmark corruption that engineers and researchers must recognize when selecting benchmarks and data vendors.

concepts.name: RL as a service for enterprises
concepts.explanation: Cai's announced venture model: providing reinforcement learning infrastructure as a service for enterprises, including managing RL datasets across base model migration with automatic post-training reruns. Enterprises stop renting lab intelligence and start owning their own.
concepts.importance: Represents an emerging product category at the intersection of post-training infrastructure and enterprise AI deployment, with significant implications for how enterprises build and maintain AI capabilities.

concepts.name: Neo labs business model
concepts.explanation: Data companies pivoting to enterprise as 'neo labs'—building abstraction layers for model routing, RL dataset management, and Antikythera mechanisms. Durable value accrues to services and app layers of actual work rather than to data labeling or model training alone.
concepts.importance: Describes the strategic evolution of AI data companies from commodity data providers to enterprise AI platform builders, informing business and engineering strategy.

concepts.name: Infrastructure pioneer market share dynamics
concepts.explanation: Cai's thesis that no infrastructure pioneer has held more than 10% market share in the long run. OpenAI and Anthropic carve fiefdoms but face pressures from anti-distillation, export controls, and enterprise exclusivity that erode dominance over time.
concepts.importance: A strategic lens for understanding AI industry dynamics and why app-layer companies should not over-index on any single model provider.

concepts.name: App-layer decoupling from model labs
concepts.explanation: GLM 5.2 surpassing GPT on real-world rubrics demonstrates that app-layer companies can decouple from model labs. Models differ on efficiency and modality, so they are not fungible like electricity, but no single lab holds permanent dominance.
concepts.importance: Validates the strategic position that application-layer AI companies can build durable value independent of any single frontier model lab, with implications for vendor strategy and build-vs-buy decisions.

concepts.name: Market maturation ordering by verifiability
concepts.explanation: AI application markets mature in verifiability order: code → search → finance → healthcare/law → cyber/bio/science → taste. This ordering follows from Verifier's Law because domains with higher verifiability (asymmetry, veracity, proliferation) are easier to train models for.
concepts.importance: Provides a predictive framework for anticipating which AI application domains will see breakthroughs next, guiding R&D investment and product roadmap decisions.

concepts.name: Modality hill problem in robotics
concepts.explanation: Robotics serves as a counterexample: the data modality is unsettled (ego-centric vs teleoperation vs UMI), vendors are unsophisticated, and vendor choices are entangled with unsolved research questions. Cai warns against dying on a modality hill.
concepts.importance: Illustrates the limits of verifiability-based market prediction when the fundamental data modality is not yet settled, cautioning engineers against premature commitment to specific data collection approaches.

concepts.name: Long-horizon dependent work as value locus
concepts.explanation: Economic value lives in deep dependent long-horizon work on the right tail of the task-horizon distribution. A threshold line moves rightward each time someone builds a real-world data pipeline, expanding the addressable frontier of automatable work.
concepts.importance: Identifies where the highest-value AI applications will emerge and why investment in long-horizon data pipelines creates compounding advantage over time.

concepts.name: Process data vs state data
concepts.explanation: State data is the saved final output used for next-token prediction (2023 paradigm); process data is the trajectory—reasoning traces, decision sequences, failures, recoveries, and verified outcomes. Cai argues process data is the scarce asset that converts generalist models into domain experts.
concepts.importance: Foundational distinction that motivates the entire talk. Understanding this separation is prerequisite for designing data pipelines that capture real expertise rather than just final answers.

concepts.name: Type one vs type two data classification
concepts.explanation: Type one data is pure capture of real workflows with minimal shaping; type two data is contrived expert-manufactured examples. Type one drives 20-to-80% model performance gains, yet vendors routinely sell type two data billed as type one.
concepts.importance: The data classification framework that data engineers must apply when procuring, validating, or building training datasets. Mislabeling has direct consequences for model quality.

concepts.name: Vendor diversification in data supply chains
concepts.explanation: AI labs mandate 20-30 different vendors for data procurement because quality does not scale linearly with quantity. This fragmentation has permanently unbundled the data supply chain, with specialists outcompeting vertically integrated giants like Scale, Surge, and Remarque.
concepts.importance: Critical for engineering teams designing data sourcing strategies. Understanding why diversification is mandated informs vendor selection, quality assurance, and pipeline architecture decisions.

concepts.name: Deterministic verifier-based benchmark construction
concepts.explanation: Cai demonstrates three real finance tasks with deterministic verifiers plus LLM-as-judge, exposing how GPT 5.5 and Opus 4.8 score within three points yet fail oppositely (arithmetic vs methodology). This approach reveals failure modes hidden by aggregate benchmark numbers.
concepts.importance: A practical engineering methodology for building evaluation harnesses that expose model-specific failure modes rather than masking them behind single composite scores.

concepts.name: Cross-harness differencing
concepts.explanation: Comparing model performance across different scaffolds and infrastructures to identify divergences. Cai argues cross-harness and cross-infrastructure differences drive benchmark divergences with hidden false positive and false negative rates in head stats.
concepts.importance: Essential evaluation engineering technique for isolating whether performance differences stem from model capability versus scaffold configuration, preventing misattribution in benchmark results.

concepts.name: Antikythera mechanism for eval translation
concepts.explanation: Cai's metaphor for bespoke systems that translate messy, domain-specific business context into runnable evaluation suites with deterministic verifiers. Named after the ancient mechanical computer, these mechanisms bridge the gap between real-world workflows and standardized evaluation.
concepts.importance: Represents a key engineering challenge in enterprise AI: building custom eval infrastructure that captures real domain complexity rather than relying on generic benchmarks.

concepts.name: Model routing abstraction layer
concepts.explanation: Enterprise infrastructure that routes requests to small or large models based on latency and performance profiles, enabling cost optimization and vendor independence. Cai argues this layer does not yet exist but will be essential as enterprises stop renting lab intelligence and own their model stack.
concepts.importance: A forward-looking engineering architecture for multi-model deployment that enterprises will need to build, representing a key opportunity for platform engineering teams.

concepts.name: RL dataset management across base model migration
concepts.explanation: Infrastructure for managing reinforcement learning datasets when underlying base models change, including automatic post-training reruns. Cai identifies this as a critical missing abstraction layer for enterprises.
concepts.importance: Addresses a core MLOps challenge: maintaining RL dataset compatibility and retraining pipelines as base models evolve, which is essential for production AI systems.

concepts.name: Live data pipeline architecture for retraining
concepts.explanation: The durable engineering moat is not static datasets but a live pipeline into real-world work plus infrastructure to keep retraining as models improve underneath. Cai argues this pipeline-plus-retraining combination is what creates defensibility.
concepts.importance: Defines the architectural pattern for building defensible AI systems: continuous data capture from live workflows feeding automatic retraining loops.

concepts.name: Long-horizon task evaluation design
concepts.explanation: Cai proposes evaluation checklists with enforced step length, heterogeneous tool calls, state transitions constraining future actions, and mandatory failure recovery to test sustained reasoning rather than isolated in-distribution questions.
concepts.importance: Provides concrete engineering criteria for constructing evaluations that measure real-world task completion rather than benchmark gaming.

concepts.name: Data supply chain unbundling
concepts.explanation: The AI data supply chain has permanently fragmented from vertically integrated giants (Scale, Surge, Remarque doing everything) to specialized vendors, driven by labs' distrust of scaling quality linearly with quantity and 20-30 vendor diversification mandates.
concepts.importance: Strategic engineering context for understanding the data procurement landscape and why single-vendor dependencies are both risky and increasingly avoidable.

concepts.name: Data market spending as engineering signal
concepts.explanation: Data market spending patterns serve as upstream indicators of lab product launches. Anthropic's cybersecurity data spending in January and biological data spending in March/April preceded Metis, Cybor, and Claude bio/life sciences launches by 2-3 months.
concepts.importance: A practical signal engineering and product teams can monitor to anticipate competitor capabilities and align their own data investment timelines.

sections.title: The data market nobody sees
sections.summary: Cai reframes data markets beyond 2019-era Manila annotation rooms, a real but least interesting ~$10-15B/year segment. The valuable data turns generalist competence into real expertise, known since 2024 when Scale was acquired and GPQA datasets were being spammed.

sections.title: Data as industrial fuel and unbundling
sections.summary: Data is to the white-collar revolution what coal and iron were to the Victorian age. The supply chain has unbundled: giants like Remarque, Surge, and Scale once did everything, but specialists now outcompete them. Fragmentation is permanent; quality does not scale linearly with quantity, so labs mandate 20-30 vendor diversification.

sections.title: Compute, data, and talent
sections.summary: Model improvement is a function of compute, data, and talent; imbalances produce inefficiency in both model performance and CapEx spend. Data is the underfunded leg that turns generalists into experts, presenting opportunity amid exponentially increasing CapEx and lagging AI revenues.

sections.title: State data versus process data and type one vs type two
sections.summary: State-based data is the saved final output (2023 next-token prediction); process-based data is the trajectory, reasoning trace, and decision sequence. Type one is pure capture of real workflows with minimal shaping; type two is contrived expert-manufactured examples. Type one drives 20-to-80% gains; everyone sells type two billed as type one.

sections.title: The three axes of verifiability
sections.summary: Jason Wei's Verifier's Law states training ease is proportional to verifiability. Cai decomposes verifiability into asymmetry, veracity, and proliferation. Coding scored high on all three via GitHub; biology, security, taste, finance, healthcare, and law score low. Markets mature in verifiability order.

sections.title: When benchmarks become snake oil
sections.summary: Contrived benchmarks are snake oil: vendors hire experts to generate tasks, cherry-pick divergences, package as hard benchmarks, then sell data to hill-climb them—Goodhart's law with profit. Contrived tests probe only isolated questions, not sustained reasoning. Cross-harness and cross-infrastructure differencing drive divergences with hidden false positive/negative rates. One benchmark number is one noisy sample—benchmark psychosis.

sections.title: Three finance benchmark tests
sections.summary: Cai runs three real finance tasks—ARR waterfall reconciliation, LBO valuation memo, and long-short pair trade—with deterministic verifiers plus LLM-as-judge. Opus 4.8 is worse than 4.7 on rubrics, over-engineering self-reflection. GPT 5.5 and Opus 4.8 score within three points but fail oppositely: GPT nails arithmetic, Opus nails methodology, revealing post-training directions.

sections.title: Predicting the next AI domain
sections.summary: Data market spending serves as an upstream indicator of lab product launches. Anthropic's heavy cybersecurity data spending in January and biological data spending in March/April preceded Metis, Cybor, and Claude bio/life sciences launches 2-3 months later. Cai offers a checklist: classify professional tasks into three verifiability axes, apply long-horizon bars with enforced step length, heterogeneous tool calls, state transitions constraining future actions, and mandatory failure recovery, then inspect raw data for five signals including sequential decisions, inferable expert actions, and independently recorded outcomes.

sections.title: The robotics counterexample
sections.summary: Robotics is a counterexample to keep analysts honest: the modality is unsettled (ego vs teleop vs UMI) and data vendors are largely unsophisticated, offering unsolicited iPhone video dumps. Vendor choices are entangled with unsolved research questions. Environment companies that succeed function as research accelerators in a boutique industry; venture scalability comes from infrastructure that serves enterprise application layer use cases, not from assuming data markets stay fixed. Don't die on a modality hill.

sections.title: Where the economic value lives
sections.summary: Cai presents a map with white-collar work share on the vertical axis and task horizon on the horizontal. Short-horizon work is addressable now, but the deep dependent long-horizon tail on the right is where real economic value and data build-out live. A threshold line moves rightward each time someone builds a real-world data pipeline. He then pivots to the model layer: no infrastructure pioneer has held more than 10% market long-term. OpenAI and Anthropic carve fiefdoms but face anti-distillation, export controls, and enterprise exclusivity pressures. GLM 5.2 surpassing GPT on real-world rubrics proves app-layer decoupling is possible; models differ on efficiency and modality, so they are not fungible like electricity.

sections.title: Why data companies move enterprise
sections.summary: Successful data companies are all pivoting to enterprise, with large enterprise revenues in unexpected ways. Once enterprises stop renting lab intelligence and start owning their own, they need an abstraction layer that doesn't yet exist: routing small models by latency and performance profiles, managing RL datasets across base model migration with automatic post-training reruns, and Antikythera mechanisms translating business context into evals. Data companies must become neo labs because durable value accrues to services and app layers of actual work.

sections.title: The durable moat
sections.summary: Two final takeaways: researchers should stop outsourcing their definition of realism to the same vendors they buy evals and tasks from—that lets the test writer grade the test. Builders' moat is not the data itself but the pipeline into real-world work plus infrastructure to keep retraining as models improve underneath. Cai announces a new venture working with real-world companies to monetize data assets and implement RL as a service for enterprises, mitigating pitfalls of companies he described.

resources.title: Asymmetry of verification and verifier's rule
resources.why: Confirms the exact formulation of Verifier's rule, its five properties (objective truth, fast to verify, scalable to verify, low noise, continuous reward), and its relation to RL environments. Validates the transcript's attribution and shows the concept originated from Jason Wei's July 2025 blog post.

resources.title: Sean Cai - LinkedIn Profile
resources.why: Confirms the speaker's identity, background in AI data markets and RL, venture investing experience, and the existence of a stealth startup matching the venture announced at the end of the talk. His LinkedIn post from ~Feb 2026 states he spent 6 months entrenched in data markets with top RLaaS teams, matching the talk's subject matter.

resources.title: Sean Cai - Personal Website
resources.why: Provides first-party confirmation of the speaker's professional identity and his focus on model economics, data markets, and investing in AI infrastructure companies.

resources.title: Sean Cai LinkedIn Post on Data Markets and RLaaS
resources.why: First-party written work by the speaker covering the same concepts as the talk (type 1 process data, RLaaS, verifiability, data market unbundling), confirming these are his established analytical positions rather than improvised talk content.

resources.title: Prime Intellect - The Open Superintelligence Stack
resources.why: Prime Intellect is an active AI infrastructure company providing 'The Open Superintelligence Stack' with RL environments, hosted evaluations, training, inference, and compute marketplace. Backed by Founders Fund, Radical, NVIDIA, Intel, Karpathy, Schulman, Dylan Patel, Clem Delangue. Customer case studies: Ramp, Zapier. Active and hiring as of August 2026.

resources.title: Surge AI - Human Intelligence for AGI
resources.why: Surge AI is an active data annotation and AI training data company providing off-the-shelf data, RL environments, expert workforce, and benchmarks. Active as of 2026. Confirmed as a real organization referenced in the transcript as a data labeling giant alongside Scale and Remarque.

resources.title: Costanoa | Early-stage venture capital firm
resources.why: Costanoa Ventures is an active early-stage venture capital firm headquartered in San Francisco and Palo Alto. Confirms the organization research description of Costanoa as a real, active VC firm where Sean Cai was on the investing team.

resources.title: Weekend Fund
resources.why: Weekend Fund is an active angel investment fund founded by Ryan Hoover (founder of Product Hunt) and Vedika Jain. Writes $200k-500k checks into early-stage startups. Active as of 2026. Confirms the organization research description.

resources.title: Scale AI Announces Next Phase of Company Evolution
resources.why: Scale AI's official blog confirms that in June 2025, Meta made a significant investment valuing Scale at over $29 billion, but Meta holds only a minority of Scale's outstanding equity. Scale AI remains an independent company. This refutes the transcript's claim that 'Scale was acquired' in 2024.

resources.title: Jason Wei - LinkedIn Profile
resources.why: Jason Wei is a Research Scientist at Meta (from July 2025), previously at OpenAI (Feb 2023 - Jul 2025) and Google (Dec 2020 - Nov 2022). Dartmouth College graduate. Confirms his movement from OpenAI to Meta and his role as originator of the verification asymmetry concept.

resources.title: Variation in Verification: Understanding Verification Dynamics in Large Language Models
resources.why: Independent academic citation confirming that Jason Wei originated the 'verification asymmetry' concept in 2025, validating the transcript's attribution of Verifier's Law to Wei.

resources.title: Amazon, Meta back Scale AI in $1 billion funding deal
resources.why: In May 2024, Scale AI raised $1 billion in a Series F funding round at $13.8 billion valuation. This was a funding round, NOT an acquisition. The transcript's claim that 'Scale was acquired' in 2024 is inaccurate.

resources.title: Zuckerberg makes Meta's biggest bet on AI, $14 billion Scale AI deal
resources.why: In June 2025, Meta finalized a $14 billion investment in Scale AI for a 49% stake. CNBC explicitly states 'By not directly acquiring Scale AI, Meta appears to be taking a similar strategy' of taking large stakes rather than outright acquisitions. Scale AI was NOT acquired.

resources.title: Meta to pay nearly $15 billion for Scale AI stake, The Information reports
resources.why: Meta agreed to take a 49% stake in Scale AI for $14.8 billion in June 2025. Scale AI was valued at $13.8 billion in spring 2024 and generated about $870 million in revenue in 2024. Scale AI was NOT acquired — Meta took a minority stake.

resources.title: Home - Remarque Systems
resources.why: Remarque Systems is a clinical trial data management company, not a data labeling or AI training data company. The transcript's reference to 'Remarque' as a data labeling giant could not be verified as referring to this organization or any other identified entity.

resources.title: Remarque
resources.why: remarque.xyz is a markdown collaboration tool, not a data labeling company. The transcript's reference to 'Remarque' as a data labeling giant could not be verified as referring to this tool or any other identified entity.

resources.title: Scale AI - The Data Platform for AI
resources.why: Scale AI is an active, independent AI data and training data company. Official website at scale.com. The transcript's claim that 'Scale was acquired' is inaccurate — Scale AI raised $1B in May 2024 and received a 49% minority investment from Meta in June 2025, but was not acquired.

resources.title: Anthropic
resources.why: Anthropic is a frontier AI model lab known for the Claude model family. Referenced in the talk for data spending patterns predicting product launches and Opus model benchmarks.

resources.title: OpenAI
resources.why: OpenAI is a frontier AI model lab known for the GPT model family. Referenced in the talk as a model lab and infrastructure pioneer whose market share thesis is discussed.

resources.title: Meta - About
resources.why: Meta (Meta Platforms, Inc.) is a diversified technology company. Referenced in the talk through Jason Wei as employer of the originator of Verifier's Law. Also confirmed as Scale AI's minority investor through Reuters and CNBC reporting.
